summary: Proposes a convention for writing 128-bit cryptographic keys in a human-readable form, using short English words. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Turn a long secret code into a few easy words so a person can read it out loud.

subtitle: Use six simple English words instead of a 64-bit hex string, and twelve words for a 128-bit key.

tldr.problem: 128-bit cryptographic keys (such as those required for SNMPv2 authentication) are difficult for humans to read, remember, and type—a long hex string like CCAC2AED591056BE4F90FD441C534766 is error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes encoding a 128-bit key as twelve English words from a standard 2048-word dictionary, reusing techniques from the S/Key one-time password system. Each key converts to a readable sequence like RASH BUSH MILK LOOK BAD BRIM AVID GAFF BAIT ROT POD LOVE.
tldr.outcome: The convention makes manual key entry more reliable and human-friendly while retaining full cryptographic strength. It is still in use in some systems today.

today: RFC 1751 is informational. The S/Key algorithm and its word-list encoding method remain in use in some systems, particularly in password and key management contexts. The 2048-word dictionary has never changed, preserving compatibility. Modern approaches to key management often use QR codes, hardware keys, or passphrases instead, but the word-encoding method is still valued in scenarios where manual entry or human communication of keys is required.

sections.title: The Problem with Binary Keys
sections.content:
Security protocols increasingly require cryptographic keys—long strings of random bits used for authentication and encryption. SNMPv2 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 2), released around the same time as this RFC, requires 128-bit keys based on the MD5 message-digest algorithm.

A 128-bit key expressed in hexadecimal (base-16) is 32 characters long: CCAC2AED591056BE4F90FD441C534766. People cannot reliably remember, read, or type such strings. Errors are common, weakening security. The RFC asks: can we represent these keys in a more human-friendly form?
sections.eli5: Secret codes for locking Internet services use random numbers and letters. A 128-bit code is really long and easy to mess up when typing, so scientists wanted a better way to show it.

sections.title: Lessons from S/Key
sections.content:
The S/Key one-time password system, designed by Phil Karn and Neil Haller, solved a related problem: it needed to represent 64-bit values in human-friendly form.

S/Key's answer was elegant: convert the 64-bit number to six English words from a dictionary of 2048 words. Since 2048 equals 2^11, six words (each representing an 11-bit value) can encode 2^66 different numbers—more than enough for a 64-bit key with parity bits. For example, the hex value EB33F77EE73D4053 becomes TIDE ITCH SLOW REIN RULE MOT.

The dictionary uses only common English words (ranging from one to four letters each) from the invariant portion of the ISO-646 character set, ensuring interoperability across systems and languages. S/Key has an installed user base, making the choice of dictionary critical: changing it would break compatibility.
sections.eli5: There is already a system called S/Key that turns small secret codes into words. It uses a list of 2048 simple words, so you can use six words instead of a long number.

sections.title: Extending S/Key to 128 Bits
sections.content:
The RFC proposes applying S/Key's approach to 128-bit keys by treating them as two 64-bit halves. Each half is converted to six words using the S/Key primitives btoe (binary to English) and etob (English to binary). New wrapper functions, key2eng and eng2key, apply these primitives twice—once for each 64-bit half.

The result is a 128-bit key encoded as twelve English words. The example in the RFC shows the 128-bit key CCAC2AED5910 56BE4F90FD441C534766 becoming RASH BUSH MILK LOOK BAD BRIM AVID GAFF BAIT ROT POD LOVE. Conversely, a user can type the twelve words and the system translates them back to a binary key: TROD MUTE TAIL WARM CHAR KONG HAAG CITY BORE O TEAL AWL becomes EFF81F9BFBC65350920CDD7416DE8009.
sections.eli5: Take the 128-bit secret code. Split it in half. Turn each half into six words using the S/Key method. Now you have twelve words—much easier to remember and type.

sections.title: How It Works in Practice
sections.content:
For successful interoperability, the dictionary must never change. The RFC includes the full source code for both the S/Key conversion routines (in C, from S/Key's original source) and the wrapper functions that extend them to 128-bit keys.

The btoe function takes an 8-byte (64-bit) value and outputs six English words. It extracts 11-bit chunks and looks them up in the Wp array (the 2048-word dictionary). The etob function reverses the process: it takes a space-separated string of six words, searches the dictionary for each, and reconstructs the 64-bit binary value. Both functions compute and verify a parity checksum over the bits, catching certain types of entry errors.

The RFC emphasizes that implementations must use the exact dictionary provided in Appendix A. A freely redistributable reference implementation is given so vendors and open-source projects can conform.
sections.eli5: The system looks up each word in a fixed list of 2048 words and converts it to numbers, or converts numbers back to words. It also checks that the result makes sense using a parity check, so typos are caught.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges a key security concern: because words are easier to remember, users might be tempted to create easy-to-guess word sequences. In particular, people might try to devise sentences or mnemonic phrases, drastically weakening security.

For instance, instead of RASH BUSH MILK LOOK BAD BRIM AVID GAFF BAIT ROT POD LOVE (random), someone might try HAPPY WARM BLUE BIRD SING TODAY FREE HOME GOOD LOVE YOU FAST—which is much weaker because it is a plausible sentence. Such weak keys are vulnerable to dictionary attacks: an attacker can try common sentence patterns before trying truly random keys.

The RFC advises that to maximize authentication strength, the twelve words must be sufficiently obscure and random. Users should avoid the temptation to devise sentences, phrases, or predictable mnemonics. The encoding itself is cryptographically secure; the weakness lies in human key generation.
sections.eli5: The danger is that people might try to use words that make a sentence, which is easier to guess. Keys have to be random nonsense, not clever sentences.
